{{also|Appendix:Variations of "dog"}} ==English== [[Image:YellowLabradorLooking.jpg|thumb|A [[domestic dog]] (a [[Labrador retriever]]) ({{taxfmt|Canis familiaris|species}})]] [[Image:African wild dog, Lycaon pictus at Savuti, Chobe National Park, Botswana.jpg|thumb|An [[African hunting dog]] ({{taxfmt|Lycaon pictus|species}})]] ===Alternative forms=== * {{alt|en|darg|dawg|dorg|dug||dialectal or pronunciation spelling}} * {{alt|en|doggie|doggy|doggy woggy|doggo||childish}} * {{alt|en|dogge||obsolete}} * {{alt|en|doge||internet slang}} ===Pronunciation=== * {{IPA|en|/dɒɡ/|a=RP}} ** {{audio|en|En-uk-dog.ogg|a=UK}} ** {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Back ache-dog.wav|a=UK}} * {{enPR|dôg|a=GA}} ** {{IPA|en|/dɔɡ/|a=lot-cloth split}} *** {{audio|en|En-us-ne-dog.ogg|a=US}} ** {{IPA|en|/dɑɡ/|a=cot-caught,dialects of Canada}} *** {{audio|en|en-us-dog.ogg|a=US,cot-caught}} * {{IPA|en|/dɒɡ/|a=CA,dialects of the US}} * {{IPA|en|/dɔɡ/|a=AU}} * {{IPA|en|/dɒɡ/|[dɔ̟ɡ]|a=NZ}} * {{IPA|en|/dɔɡ/|a=Scotland}} * {{IPA|en|/dɑɡ/|a=South Africa}} * {{rhymes|en|ɒɡ|s=1}} ===Etymology 1=== {{wikidata lexeme|L1122}} {{etymon|en|id=canine|:inh|enm:dogge|tree=1}} {{inh+|en|enm|dogge}}Hans Kurath, Sherman M. Kuhn, ''Middle English Dictionary'' (1962, {{ISBN|0472010441}}), page 4, page 1204 (akin to {{cog|sco|dug}}), from {{inh|en|ang|docga,*dogga}},{{R:ang:BT|docga}}Laurel Brinton, Alexander Bergs, ''Old English'' (2017, {{ISBN|3110525305}}), page 59: "In addition, the velar [ɡɡ] and palatal [ɡɡj] geminates could be written as or , as in ~ ..."; Richard M. Hogg, Norman Francis Blake, ''The Cambridge History of the English Language'' (1992, {{ISBN|052126474X}}), volume 1, age 91 says much the same. of {{unc|en|nocap=1}} origin.{{cite-web |en |url=https://www.npr.org/2025/08/13/nx-s1-5500476/dog-history-etymology-origin |title=Why the origin of the word 'dog' remains a mystery |work={{w|All Things Considered}} |date=2025-08-13 |accessdate=2025-08-18 |first=Juliana |last=Kim |publisher={{w|NPR}}}} The original meaning seems to have been a common dog, as opposed to a well-bred one, or something like '[[cur]]', and perhaps later came to be used for stocky dogs. Possibly a pet-form diminutive with suffix {{m|ang|-ga}} (compare {{m|ang|frocga|t=frog}}, {{m|ang|*picga|t=pig}}), appended to a base {{m|ang|*dog-}}, {{m|ang|*doc-}} of unclear origin and meaning. One possibility is {{der|en|ang|dox|t=dark, swarthy}} (compare {{m|ang|frocga}} from {{m|ang|frox}}).Piotr Gąsiorowski, 2006. [https://repozytorium.amu.edu.pl/jspui/bitstream/10593/2479/1/Dogga.pdf The Etymology of Old English *docga]. ''Indogermanische Forschungen'', 111. Another proposal is that it derives from {{cog|gmw-pro|*dugan||to be suitable}}, the origin of {{cog|ang|dugan||to be good, worthy, useful}}, {{cog|en|dow}}, {{cog|nl|deugen}}, {{cog|de|taugen}}. The theory goes that it could have been an epithet for dogs, commonly used by children, meaning "good/useful animal".[https://www.oed.com/view/Entry/56405] Another one is that it is related to {{m|ang|*docce|t=stock, muscle}}, from {{m+|gmw-pro|*dokkā|id=bundle|t=round mass, ball, muscle, doll}}, whence {{m+|en|dock|id=cut|t=stumpy tail}}. In 14th-century England, {{m|en|hound}} (from {{m+|ang|hund}}) was the general word for all domestic canines, and ''dog'' referred to a subtype resembling the modern mastiff and bulldog.[http://hrcak.srce.hr/index.php?show=clanak&id_clanak_jezik=48370&lang=en] By the 16th century, ''dog'' had become the general word, and ''hound'' had begun to refer only to breeds used for [[hunt]]ing.[https://books.google.com/?id=uZcs6poXkfEC&pg=PA215] In the 16th century, the word ''dog'' was adopted by several continental European languages as their word for {{m|en|mastiff}}.{{R:Online Etymology Dictionary|dog}} Despite similarities in forms and meaning, it is not related to {{noncog|vmb|dog}}. ====Noun==== {{wikidata lexeme|L1122}} {{en-noun|~}} # A [[mammal]] of the [[family]] {{taxfmt|Canidae|family}}: ## {{senseid|en|Q144}} The [[species]] {{taxfmt|Canis familiaris|species}} (sometimes designated {{taxfmt|Canis lupus familiaris|subspecies}}), [[domesticated]] for thousands of [[years]] and of highly variable appearance because of [[human]] breeding. ##: {{hyper|en|canid|<|mammal|<|vertebrate|<|animal|<|organism|<|creature#Noun}} ##: {{ux|en|The '''dog''' barked all night long.}} ##* {{RQ:Ouida Puck|volume=I|chapter=Introduction. His First Paper.|page=2|passage={{...}} I beg again to state, in my humility, that I am Only a '''Dog'''. Such a little '''dog''' too. {{...}} I am very white, very woolly, very pretty indeed; covered all over with snowy curls, and having two bright black eyes and a black shiny tip to my nose like patent leather.}} ##* {{RQ:Maxwell Mirror and the Lamp|chapter=16|passage=The preposterous altruism too!{{...}}Resist not evil. It is an insane immolation of self—as bad intrinsically as fakirs stabbing themselves or anchorites warping their spines in caves scarcely large enough for a fair-sized '''dog'''.}} ##* {{RQ:Allingham China Governess|chapter=19|passage=When Timothy and Julia hurried up the staircase to the bedroom floor, where a considerable commotion was taking place, Tim took Barry Leach with him.{{nb...}}. The captive made no resistance and came not only quietly but in a series of eager little rushes like a timid '''dog''' on a choke chain.}} ## {{senseid|en|Q25324}} Any member of the family Canidae, including domestic dogs, [[wolf|wolves]], [[fox|foxes]], [[coyote]]s, [[jackal]]s, and their relatives {{q|extant and extinct}}. ##: {{syn|en|canid}} ##: {{hyper|en|mammal|<|vertebrate|<|animal|<|organism|<|creature#Noun}} ##* {{quote-text|en|year=1989|author=John L. Gittleman|title=Carnivore Behavior, Ecology, and Evolution|page=561|passage=This includes the development of hyena-like bone crushers (''Osteoborus'' and ''Borophagus''), a large bone-crushing hunting '''dog''' (''Aelurodon''), and another borophagine frugivorous '''dog''' (''Carpocyon'').}} ## {{lb|en|often|attributive}} A male dog, [[wolf]], or [[fox]], as opposed to a [[bitch]] or [[vixen]]. ##* {{quote-journal|en|journal=Dogdom|volume=9|year=1908|page=337|column=1|passage=Entirely disregarding sex, Ch. '''Books''' and '''books''' and '''books'''. And then, just when an observer might be lured into thinking that that must be it, more '''books'''...
